transcript:
Header:
Date: 2027-01-12
Start: 15:30 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Lena, Marcus, Priya (Redwood) — Daniel, Marta, Omar, Sana (Aurelius)

Summary: quick technical deep dive on throughput safety — focused on prefill/hysteresis for KV cache, continuous batching safety knobs, max_num_seqs and token caps, and a quantization fallback path for on-prem constrained GPUs. customer concerned about onprem noisy neighbors and data residency.

Topics: prefill hysteresis, continuous batching windowing, max_num_seqs ceiling, token caps, int4 quant fallback, VPC peering constraints, bench harness plan

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Lena Ortiz: Hey all, thanks for carving time. We're gonna dig into the prefill hysteresis idea and how to keep continuous batching from oscillating when onprem nodes are noisy. Marcus is gonna run most of the tech.
[00:14] Marcus Hale: Hey, hi. quick note — I might jumble a few acronyms, but i'll try to be clear. The core problem you hit is, when KV hitrate drops, the scheduler sees smaller seq groups so the max_num_seqs policy can cause a flurry of smaller batches and that triggers CPU/GPU context thrash, which looks like oscillation.
[00:31] Daniel Cho: yeah, exactly. our cluster showed these bursty latency tails, sometimes 300–500ms higher when background ETL spikes. We run onprem with a constrained NIC and can't just add more capacity.
[00:45] Marcus Hale: Right. So our two-pronged approach: 1) prefill hysteresis — keep a lightweight background KV warmup that only triggers when hitrate drops below a low threshold for X seconds, and 2) scheduler hysteresis knobs — a decay window on max_num_seqs adjustments so the scheduler doesn't immediately reduce target seqs on a transient drop.
[01:02] Marta Ruiz: when you say "prefill" do you mean pulling full KV pages for all clients? Curious about memory blow up.
[01:10] Priya Raman: good question. No, not full pages. prefill is prioritized partial prefetch — we store a short LRU of top-k prefixes per customer shard and only fetch them asynchronously, capped by a token budget and memory cap. The hysteresis bit prevents repeated evict/re-prefetch cycles.
[01:24] Omar El-Sayed: so we set a low water and high water threshold? like if hitrate < 60% for 30s start prefill until it recovers above 75%?
[01:33] Marcus Hale: Exactly, something like that. We expose env vars: PREFILL_LOW=0.6, PREFILL_HIGH=0.75, PREFILL_DURATION_SEC=30. Those numbers are tunable. Also prefetch rate limit so it doesn't saturate NIC.
[01:44] Daniel Cho: ok that sounds reasonable. How about continuous batching changes? we saw the scheduler quickly drop max_num_seqs to 1 and throughput collapsed.
[01:54] Marcus Hale: The scheduler observes windowed seq statistics over two timescales: fast (3–5s) and slow (30–60s). We add a softness factor so fast changes only influence up to X% of the current max_num_seqs. The slow window enforces the long term. So if your ETL spike is short, you won't immediately fragment batches.
[02:11] Marta Ruiz: Can we see the exact knobs? we need something we can commit into our runbook.
[02:16] Marcus Hale: Sure — knobs we typically tune: MAX_NUM_SEQS_DEFAULT, MAX_NUM_SEQS_MIN, MAX_NUM_SEQS_DECAY_RATE, FAST_WINDOW_SEC, SLOW_WINDOW_SEC, SOFT_CHANGE_PCT. Example defaults: DEFAULT=64, MIN=8, DECAY=0.75, FAST_WINDOW=5, SLOW_WINDOW=45, SOFT_PCT=0.2. We'll share a table after.
[02:34] Sana Patel: From security side, any prefill touches customer tokens — do you encrypt those caches and will data leave the VPC?
[02:42] Priya Raman: Prefill operates inside the serving plane — on onprem deployment it stays inside your VPC. We use envelope encryption with your KMS when configured; K/V pages are persisted encrypted at rest. We'll include the KMS/HSM integration docs.
[02:56] Daniel Cho: quantization — our onprem GPUs are tight on mem; we were considering int4 but worried about hallucination/regression. we saw a quality drop in an early experiment. how do you handle fallback?
[03:10] Marcus Hale: Two levels: offline model calibration and runtime safety. Offline: we run evals and measure quality delta across prompts — some models degrade with int4 on certain tokens. Runtime: we implement a quant_fallback path — when generation quality metrics (like perplexity delta or specific prompt checks) cross a threshold, we route that request to a higher-precision variant or to a different shard with a fuller-precision model.
[03:31] Marta Ruiz: that routing could increase tail latency for those requests, correct?
[03:34] Marcus Hale: yes, but it's selective. Also we can do hybrid decoding: run int4 path for prefix and switch to fp16 for the final N tokens. That reduces memory but preserves critical output quality.
[03:46] Omar El-Sayed: how do we detect quality regressions at runtime? we can't run human evals live.
[03:51] Priya Raman: we use a small set of lightweight automatic checks: log-prob delta from baseline, repetition ratio, and a prompt-specific guard set you provide (safety or correctness queries). If a request trips the guard, we mark it for fallback. We'll share the guard SDK.
[04:06] Daniel Cho: costs — this sounds like extra compute. our finance team will push back.
[04:10] Lena Ortiz: good point. tradeoff: cost of selective fallback vs cost of rework for bad outputs or regulatory risk in healthcare. We can show expected additional % of high-precision fallbacks from our past customers — typically single-digit percent of requests after calibration.
[04:25] Daniel Cho: ok. For our baseline perf tests, what harness should we run to reproduce the oscillation?
[04:31] Marcus Hale: We'll give you a bench harness — it simulates peaky background load, KV miss patterns, and runs a steady RPS. Important knobs: sequence length distribution, prefix reuse (controls hitrate), and background CPU/IO noise.
[04:45] Marcus Hale: Suggestion: run three experiments — baseline (no prefill/hysteresis), prefill-only, prefill + scheduler knobs + quant fallback hybrid. Collect p50/p90/p99 latency, GPU utilization, KV hitrate, batch size distribution, and max_num_seqs over time.
[04:59] Marta Ruiz: are there any known regressions between prefill and eviction frequency? e.g., prefill causes K/V churn?
[05:06] Priya Raman: prefills are pre-prioritized by LRU weight — we favor high-value prefixes. If your working set is massive, prefill won't attempt the whole set; it obeys a memory cap and token cap. Also hysteresis is designed to prevent tight evict-prefill cycles.
[05:22] Omar El-Sayed: VPC peering — our security team is strict. We need details on what ports and subnets Redwood will need for the private control plane and how to set up flow logs.
[05:31] Lena Ortiz: We'll send our deployment checklist. For private deployments we require control-plane egress to our management endpoint on port 443 only; data plane can be fully isolated. We'll include a diagram and the exact CIDR list.
[05:44] Sana Patel: SOC2 artifacts? encryption, RBAC, audit logs?
[05:48] Lena Ortiz: yes, will attach SOC2 Type II summary, audit log retention options, and RBAC screenshots.
[05:55] Daniel Cho: back to token caps — our app sometimes sends long contexts (6k tokens). how do token limits interplay with batching?
[06:03] Marcus Hale: Long contexts increase token compute and reduce batch packing efficiency. We recommend a per-request token ceiling that maps to a bucketed scheduling lane — requests over X tokens get routed to a high-precision/large-seq pool with separate max_num_seqs. This avoids blocking short requests.
[06:21] Marta Ruiz: so we create small and large lanes?
[06:24] Marcus Hale: Exactly. Typical configuration: small lane max_num_seqs 64, large lane 8–12. And a token_limit env var — e.g., TOKEN_LANE_BOUNDARY=2048. Requests <=2048 go small lane, >2048 go large lane.
[06:36] Omar El-Sayed: How do you handle ingress rate spikes — do you backpressure?
[06:40] Priya Raman: We support token-level quotas and soft-deny: we can queue up to a configurable window, then shed or downgrade to lower-precision variants. There's also a graceful fallback to hosted endpoints if onprem is bursting and you allow peering.
[06:54] Daniel Cho: we do not want data leaving the VPC. fallback to hosted is not allowed.
[06:58] Lena Ortiz: Understood. We'll keep the fallback options internal to your cluster — route to fp16 shards or stall with retry. We'll document options.
[07:06] Marcus Hale: One more operational tip — expose metrics: batch_size_histogram, seq_group_count, kv_hitrate, prefill_queue_size, max_num_seqs_effective. These help tune knobs quickly. We'll share a Grafana dashboard.
[07:20] Marta Ruiz: great. could you send a sample PromQL for kv hitrate and effective max_num_seqs?
[07:24] Marcus Hale: Sure: kv_hitrate = sum(kv_hits)/sum(kv_lookups) over 1m; max_num_seqs_effective = avg_over_time(scheduler_max_num_seqs[1m]). We'll include exact metric names.
[07:36] Daniel Cho: timeline — if we approve, how fast can we run a pilot?
[07:40] Lena Ortiz: We can spin the test harness in ~48 hours after we get VPC details; bench run usually 24–72 hours depending on scale. Full pilot with guard calibration ~2–3 weeks.
[07:50] Marcus Hale: I'll prepare a minimal config that you can drop into your onprem helm/compose to enable prefill_hysteresis=false->true flip, and a set of test scripts.
[07:59] Marta Ruiz: anything else we should watch out for?
[08:02] Priya Raman: watch eviction storms — if you see repeated eviction cycles increase IO, raise PREFILL_DURATION_SEC and lower prefill parallelism. Also check GPU memory fragmentation when using hybrid quantization.
[08:14] Daniel Cho: can you quantify typical % of fallbacks for healthcare customers? you mentioned single digits.
[08:20] Lena Ortiz: In our experience across a few regulated customers, after calibration it's typically 2–7% of requests hitting fallback, concentrated in certain prompts. We'll send anonymized stats.
[08:30] Marta Ruiz: ok let's recap next steps.
[08:33] Lena Ortiz: Recap: Redwood sends prefill/hysteresis config examples, bench harness, Prom dashboards, SOC2 bundle. Aurelius provisions VPC test and shares subnets. Marcus and Omar will coordinate on run details. We'll schedule a follow-up next Thursday.
[08:50] Daniel Cho: sounds good. thanks everyone.

[End of call]
